docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The core has no dependencies; the duckdb extra adds the database this example uses.

pip install "factlang[duckdb]"

docs.title: Build a shop to check
docs.text:
500 customers and 2,000 orders, with a few things wrong on purpose.

import duckdb
import factlang as fl

conn = duckdb.connect()
conn.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE customers AS
    SELECT i AS id,
           CASE WHEN i % 25 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE 'customer' || i || '@example.com' END AS email
    FROM range(1, 501) AS t(i)
""")
conn.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE orders AS
    SELECT i AS id,
           CASE WHEN i % 160 = 0 THEN 10000 + i ELSE 1 + (i * 7) % 500 END AS customer_id,
           CASE i % 10 WHEN 0 THEN 'refunded' WHEN 1 THEN 'open' WHEN 2 THEN 'open'
                       ELSE 'paid' END AS status,
           CAST(5 + (i * 37) % 200 AS DECIMAL(10, 2)) AS amount,
           CASE WHEN i % 10 IN (1, 2) THEN NULL
                ELSE current_date - CAST(i % 30 AS INTEGER) END AS shipped_at
    FROM range(1, 2001) AS t(i)
""")

connector = fl.DBAPIConnector(conn, "duckdb")

docs.title: Check what an analyst said
docs.text:
report = fl.Checker(connector).check("""
JOIN orders.customer_id -> customers.id CARD N:1 MATCH >=99%
NULLS customers.email RATE <=5%
VALUES orders.status IN ['paid', 'open', 'shipped']
""")
for outcome in report.outcomes:
    print(f"{outcome.verdict.value:5} {outcome.explanation}")

fail  match_rate 0.9765625 < 0.99
pass  null_rate 0.04 <= 0.05
fail  undeclared_rows 200 != 0

docs.title: Agents and LLMs
docs.text: FactLang was designed for the claims AI agents make. An agent that answers questions over a warehouse can write the numbers in its answer as FactLang, check them, and only state what held. Everything an agent needs is generated from the active verb pack, so it cannot drift from what the analyser accepts.

docs.title: Tool definitions
docs.text:
import factlang as fl
from factlang.agent import tool_definitions, handle_tool_call

tools = tool_definitions()          # three JSON-schema tool specs
print([t["name"] for t in tools])   # ['factlang_check', 'factlang_lint', 'factlang_explain']
tool arguments does factlang_check claims measures every claim and returns one outcome per claim, with facts and SQL evidence factlang_lint claims validates without touching the warehouse: diagnostics with codes, positions, hints and suggestions factlang_explain claims, dialect the SQL each claim would run, without executing anything

Each spec is {"name", "description", "input_schema"}. The factlang_check description embeds the compact verb reference, so the model sees the verbs, their attributes and two examples each. Adapt the dict to your LLM API's tool format (for example rename input_schema to parameters).

docs.title: Dispatching tool calls
docs.text:
handle_tool_call(name, arguments, checker) runs one call and returns a JSON-safe dict. It never raises: bad arguments, an unknown tool or an internal failure come back as {"error": {"code", "message", "tool"}}.

checker = fl.Checker(dialect="postgres")      # no warehouse: lint and explain still work
result = handle_tool_call("factlang_lint", {"claims": "UNIQE orders.id"}, checker)
print(result["diagnostics"][0]["suggestion"])  # UNIQUE

A typical loop: the model drafts claims, calls factlang_lint until they are clean, then factlang_check; your host keeps the sentences whose claims passed and rewrites or drops the rest. The factlang_check result is Report.to_dict(), and its first key is verified: true only when every measurable claim was measured and passed. ok is weaker (it is still true with no_data outcomes or nothing measured), so gate on verified. Outcomes carry a semantic hash, so a host can cache verdicts per fact.

docs.title: The verb reference for prompts
docs.text:
from factlang.agent import verb_reference

system_prompt = "You can verify facts with FactLang.\n\n" + verb_reference(style="compact")

style="markdown" is the full reference (the verb reference page is built from the same contracts); style="compact" is a few lines per verb. Both take a pack argument, so custom verbs appear automatically.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
With the extra factlang[mcp], the same three tools are served over MCP on stdio:

pip install "factlang[mcp,sqlalchemy]"
export FACTLANG_DSN="postgresql+psycopg://reader@warehouse/shop"
factlang mcp                          # the URL comes from FACTLANG_DSN
factlang mcp --dialect snowflake      # no warehouse: lint and explain only

Options: --timeout (per-probe seconds, default 60), --max-bytes (refuse probes priced above this by a dry run), --max-claims (default 200), --name (the server name). Without a DSN, factlang_check answers with a no_connector error. python -m factlang.agent.mcp is the same server.

--max-bytes only bounds cost on connectors that can price a query without running it (BigQuery does); elsewhere it does nothing. --max-claims N is what bounds the work: a factlang_check or factlang_explain call carrying more than N claims is refused with the error code too_many_claims, before any analysis or SQL. Claims are counted by lines: blank lines, comment-only lines and USE directives do not count, and \ continuations join lines first. factlang_lint is not capped, since it runs no SQL. The same cap is the max_claims= keyword of handle_tool_call (default 200; None removes it).

Error codes can grow

The tool error codes (unknown_tool, invalid_arguments, unknown_dialect, no_connector, too_many_claims, internal_error) may be added to in patch releases. Handle an unknown code as a generic failure.

Register it with your MCP client as a stdio command, e.g. factlang mcp with FACTLANG_DSN in the server's environment. Run the server under a read-only database role: FactLang's probes are SELECT-only, and the credentials are what guarantee the rest.

Credentials on the command line

A DSN with a password on the command line is visible to other users of the machine in the process list. factlang check and factlang mcp both read FACTLANG_DSN from the environment when neither --dsn nor (check) --connector / (mcp) --dialect is given; prefer that.

docs.title: Grounding evaluations
docs.text: For LLM evaluation, score an answer by whether its facts hold: have the model emit claims alongside its answer, check them, and count pass against fail. Treat no_data, error and invalid separately: they mean "not established", not "wrong".

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Installing FactLang installs the factlang command (also python -m factlang). It uses only the standard library; check needs a way to reach your warehouse.

factlang lint FILE...                      report diagnostics; never executes
factlang fmt [--check] FILE...             rewrite files in canonical form
factlang explain --dialect D FILE          print each claim's SQL
factlang check [--dsn URL | --connector MODULE:ATTR] [--dialect D] FILE
factlang verbs [--json]                    list the verbs of the standard pack
factlang mcp [--dsn URL | --dialect D]     serve the tools over MCP on stdio

--format text|json|markdown chooses the output and may come before or after the subcommand. Any FILE may be - to read standard input; fmt - prints the canonical form instead of rewriting a file.

docs.title: lint
docs.text:
factlang lint contracts/*.fl
cat facts.fl | factlang lint --format json -

Parses and analyses every file with the standard pack and prints caret diagnostics. Nothing is executed and no warehouse is needed, so it is the right check for a pre-commit hook.

docs.title: fmt
docs.text:
factlang fmt facts.fl            # rewrite in place
factlang fmt --check facts.fl    # exit 1 if the file would change (for CI)

docs.title: explain
docs.text:
factlang explain --dialect bigquery facts.fl

-- UNIQUE orders.id
SELECT a.non_null AS non_null, ... FROM orders ...;

-- ROWS orders VALUE>=1
SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM orders;

The SQL is the display form, literals inlined; a literal that cannot be inlined safely (a backslash or NUL in a string, for example) is left as its {{name}} placeholder, with the value listed under params in --format json. Any native dialect works, and with factlang[sqlglot] installed any dialect sqlglot knows.

docs.title: check
docs.text:
export FACTLANG_DSN="postgresql+psycopg://reader@warehouse/shop"
factlang check facts.fl
factlang check --format markdown facts.fl > report.md
factlang check --connector myproject.warehouse:connector facts.fl

The warehouse comes from one of:

  • --dsn URL: a SQLAlchemy URL (needs factlang[sqlalchemy] and the driver);
  • FACTLANG_DSN: the same URL from the environment, used when neither --dsn nor --connector is given;
  • --connector module:attr: a Connector, a factory returning one, or a DB-API connection (then give --dialect). This imports and runs module as ordinary Python code, with the current working directory added to sys.path, so only name a module you trust and run the command from a directory you trust.

Keep credentials off the command line

A URL with a password passed as --dsn is visible to other users of the machine in the process list. Put it in FACTLANG_DSN, or use --connector with code that reads your secret store.

The last line of the text output sums the report up and agrees with the exit code: verified: 6 PASS (exit 0), ok, nothing verified: no claims (exit 0, nothing was measurable: an empty file or only unprobeable claims) or not verified: 1 NO_DATA (any non-zero exit). The JSON and Markdown reports carry verified and ok; see Verdicts.

docs.title: verbs
docs.text:
factlang verbs           # one line per verb
factlang verbs --json    # machine-readable signatures

docs.title: mcp
docs.text: Serves factlang_check, factlang_lint and factlang_explain over MCP on stdio; needs factlang[mcp]. The warehouse URL comes from --dsn or, when neither --dsn nor --dialect is given, from FACTLANG_DSN; with none of the three it exits 2. See Agents and LLMs.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
code meaning 0 every claim passed (or is unprobeable) 1 a claim failed; for fmt --check, a file would be reformatted 2 invalid input: bad usage, an unreadable file, a claim or directive with front-end errors, a connector that cannot be loaded 3 errors or undecidable: an error or no_data outcome, a claim that cannot be rendered

When several apply, 2 wins over 1, and 1 over 3. In CI, factlang check facts.fl alone fails the job on any failed or unmeasurable claim.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page takes you from pip install to a report of verdicts in about five minutes. It uses an in-memory DuckDB database so you need no warehouse; every code block on this page is executed by the test suite, in order, so what you see is what you get.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install factlang            # the core: no dependencies at all
pip install "factlang[duckdb]"  # plus DuckDB, used on this page

Other extras add a driver for your warehouse: bigquery, snowflake, redshift, databricks, postgres, mysql, clickhouse, mssql, oracle, trino, plus sqlalchemy, sqlglot (the long tail of dialects) and mcp (the MCP server). all installs every one of them.

docs.title: A shop to check
docs.text:
Build a small shop: 500 customers and 2,000 orders. A few things are wrong with it on purpose: twelve orders point at customers that do not exist, and some orders are refunded, a status nobody mentioned.

import duckdb
import factlang as fl

conn = duckdb.connect()
conn.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE customers AS
    SELECT i AS id,
           CASE WHEN i % 25 = 0 THEN NULL ELSE 'customer' || i || '@example.com' END AS email
    FROM range(1, 501) AS t(i)
""")
conn.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE orders AS
    SELECT i AS id,
           CASE WHEN i % 160 = 0 THEN 10000 + i ELSE 1 + (i * 7) % 500 END AS customer_id,
           CASE i % 10 WHEN 0 THEN 'refunded' WHEN 1 THEN 'open' WHEN 2 THEN 'open'
                       ELSE 'paid' END AS status,
           CAST(5 + (i * 37) % 200 AS DECIMAL(10, 2)) AS amount,
           CASE WHEN i % 10 IN (1, 2) THEN NULL
                ELSE current_date - CAST(i % 30 AS INTEGER) END AS shipped_at
    FROM range(1, 2001) AS t(i)
""")

connector = fl.DBAPIConnector(conn, "duckdb")

DBAPIConnector wraps any PEP 249 connection: psycopg, snowflake-connector, pyodbc, oracledb, the Databricks and Trino drivers and so on. The second argument names the SQL dialect FactLang should write.

docs.title: One claim, one call
docs.text:
outcome = fl.check("UNIQUE orders.id", connector=connector)

print(outcome.verdict)       # Verdict.PASS
print(outcome.explanation)   # max_rows_per_key 1 <= 1
assert outcome.verdict is fl.Verdict.PASS

fl.check returns an Outcome when the text holds exactly one claim. The explanation always names the numbers the verdict was decided on.

docs.title: Many claims, one report
docs.text:
Claims are line-oriented: one per line, # starts a comment.

claims = """
# what an analyst told us about the shop
JOIN orders.customer_id -> customers.id CARD N:1 MATCH >=99%
NULLS customers.email RATE <=5%
VALUES orders.status IN ['paid', 'open', 'shipped']
COUNT orders VALUE ==1400 WHERE status = 'paid'
SUM orders.amount VALUE ==209000 TOLERANCE 1%
FRESH orders.shipped_at WITHIN 2d
"""

checker = fl.Checker(connector)
report = checker.check(claims)

for o in report.outcomes:
    print(f"{o.verdict.value:8} {o.claim_text}\n         {o.explanation}")

assert [o.verdict.value for o in report.outcomes] == [
    "fail", "pass", "fail", "pass", "pass", "pass",
]
assert not report.ok and not report.verified

The output reads:

fail     JOIN orders.customer_id -> customers.id CARD N:1 MATCH >=99%
         match_rate 0.9765625 < 0.99
pass     NULLS customers.email RATE <=5%
         null_rate 0.04 <= 0.05
fail     VALUES orders.status IN ['paid', 'open', 'shipped']
         undeclared_rows 200 != 0
pass     COUNT orders VALUE ==1400 WHERE status = 'paid'
         value 1400 == 1400
pass     SUM orders.amount VALUE ==209000 TOLERANCE 1%
         value 209000 satisfies == 209000 (band 2090)
pass     FRESH orders.shipped_at WITHIN 2d
         age_seconds … <= 172800

Two of the analyst's statements were wrong. The report says exactly how wrong:

join, _, values, *_ = report.outcomes
print(join.facts["matched"], "of", join.facts["distinct_left"], "customer ids match")
print(values.facts["top_undeclared"])
assert join.facts["distinct_left"] == 512
assert values.facts["top_undeclared"][0]["value"] == "refunded"

facts holds every number the verb measured, not only the one it was judged on. A JOIN also reports coverage (how much of the right side is reached), row_match_rate and the key multiplicities; see Standard verbs.

docs.title: Look at the evidence
docs.text:
Every measured outcome carries the SQL that produced it:

evidence = report.outcomes[3].evidence
print(evidence.sql)      # SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid'
print(evidence.params)   # ('paid',)
print(evidence.dialect, evidence.tier)   # duckdb verified
assert evidence.params == ("paid",)

evidence.sql is the display form, with literals inlined so you can paste it into a SQL console (a value it cannot inline safely is left as a {{name}} placeholder; see Evidence). What actually ran was a parameterised statement: 'paid' travelled as a typed bind parameter (evidence.params), never as SQL text. That holds for every literal in every claim, which is why a claim cannot inject SQL.

docs.title: Reports for people and machines
docs.text:
print(report.to_markdown())
data = report.to_dict()             # JSON-ready; report.to_json() gives the text
assert data["verified"] is False and data["ok"] is False
assert data["summary"]["pass"] == 4 and data["summary"]["fail"] == 2

docs.title: Mistakes are diagnostics, not exceptions
docs.text:
FactLang never raises on bad input. It reports a coded diagnostic with a caret and, where it can, a suggestion:

bag = fl.lint("UNIQE orders.id\nNULLS customers.email RATE <=120%\n")
print(bag.render())
assert bag.codes() == ["FL300", "FL309"]

error[FL300]: unknown verb UNIQE
  --> 1:1
UNIQE orders.id
^^^^^
did you mean: UNIQUE?

error[FL309]: RATE: ratio must be between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%), got 1.2
  --> 2:30
NULLS customers.email RATE <=120%
                             ^^^^

Every code is listed in the diagnostics reference. Inside a report, an invalid claim is an invalid outcome and the other claims still run.

docs.title: No warehouse? Compile instead
docs.text:
fl.compile renders the SQL for any dialect without connecting to anything. This is what the playground's Explain SQL does; its Check runs the claims for real, on DuckDB in your browser.

for probe in fl.compile("NULLS customers.email RATE <=5%", dialect="snowflake"):
    print(probe.inline())       # display-oriented: literals inlined, or FL507 if unsafe

probe.sql_template and probe.params are the executable form; probe.bind("qmark") (or numeric, named, format, pyformat) produces the driver's spelling.

docs.title: What you can try
docs.text:
• Check runs the claims on the tables listed under Data and shows a card per claim: its verdict, the measured numbers, the reason, the SQL with its bound parameters and how long it took. Check always runs on DuckDB, whatever the dialect menu says. A query gets 30 seconds; past that the claim is ERROR (FL702) and the database is restarted.
  • Lint parses and analyses the claims against the standard verbs and prints every diagnostic with a caret, its code and a suggestion when there is one. Once the database has started, table and column names are checked against the loaded tables too.
  • Format prints the canonical form: the spelling FactLang hashes and stores.
  • Explain SQL shows each claim's query for the chosen dialect, its bind parameters and the dialect's tier. Switch dialects to see how COUNT_BIG, TOP, COUNTIF or FILTER (WHERE …) replace each other while the meaning stays the same.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
The sample shop is the database of Getting started: 500 customers and 2,000 orders. The two Sample shop examples run on it; the first is the claim ledger on the home page.

Load CSV (or drop files on the Data panel) adds each file as a table next to the sample tables. The table name comes from the file name: its last extension is dropped, it is lower-cased, every character other than a letter, a digit or an underscore becomes an underscore, a name starting with a digit gets the prefix t_, and a name already loaded gets _2, _3, … appended. So 2024 Sales.v2.csv becomes t_2024_sales_v2. Columns keep their CSV names; each one is listed with the way a claim writes it. The files are read by DuckDB inside your browser tab and never uploaded, and a share link carries the claims only, never your data. After loading, the panel offers suggested claims about the new table: starting points, not facts, so some of them can fail.

To run claims against your own warehouse, install FactLang and follow Getting started.

docs.title: Catalogs
docs.text:
A catalog answers two questions about a table: does it exist, and what are its columns and types. The analyser uses it to catch misspelt names (FL311) and type mismatches (FL312, FL305), and the structure verbs EXISTS and TYPE are answered from it. Every code block on this page runs in the test suite.

class Catalog(Protocol):
    def table_exists(self, ref: TableRef) -> bool | None: ...      # None = unknown
    def columns(self, ref: TableRef) -> dict[str, str] | None: ...  # name -> type

Unknown is not an error. A catalog that cannot answer returns None. The analyser reports FL311 only on a definite "no", and an FL313 information note when it could not check; a structure verb whose catalog cannot answer is no_data, never a pass or a fail.

docs.title: The ones that ship
docs.text:
catalog fl.NullCatalog() knows nothing; skips name checks fl.StaticCatalog({"orders": {"id": "integer", …}}) authoritative, from a dict; StaticCatalog.from_json(path) reads a JSON file of the same shape fl.WarehouseCatalog(connector) asks the warehouse's INFORMATION_SCHEMA (or equivalent), one query per table, only for tables the claims mention; never enumerates schemas fl.CachedCatalog(inner, ttl_s=300, max_tables=10_000) a thread-safe TTL + LRU cache over any catalog, unknown answers included

A Checker with a connector and no catalog builds CachedCatalog(WarehouseCatalog(connector)) itself. checker.offline_catalog() returns the catalog to use when nothing may be executed (the host's own, or None when the Checker built a warehouse catalog), which is what you pass to a sibling Checker that only compiles for another dialect.

import factlang as fl

catalog = fl.StaticCatalog({
    "orders": {"id": "integer", "customer_id": "integer", "status": "varchar"},
    "customers": {"id": "integer", "email": "varchar"},
})
print(fl.lint("UNIQUE orders.stauts", catalog=catalog).render())
assert fl.lint("UNIQUE orders.stauts", catalog=catalog).codes() == ["FL311"]
assert fl.lint("JOIN orders.customer_id -> customers.email MATCH >=99%",
               catalog=catalog).codes() == ["FL312"]

In a StaticCatalog, unquoted parts of a reference match case-insensitively and quoted parts exactly; the fullest key (catalog.schema.table, then schema.table, then table) is tried first.

docs.title: Writing a catalog
docs.text:
Any object with the two methods works, for example one backed by your schema registry:

class RegistryCatalog:
    def __init__(self, registry):
        self.registry = registry

    def table_exists(self, ref):
        return ref.table.text in self.registry

    def columns(self, ref):
        return self.registry.get(ref.table.text)

catalog = fl.CachedCatalog(RegistryCatalog({"orders": {"id": "integer"}}))
assert fl.lint("ROWS shipments VALUE >=1", catalog=catalog).codes() == ["FL311"]

Return None whenever you do not know. Returning False or omitting a column for a table you do not actually know about turns your catalog's ignorance into a user-facing error.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text: Only connectors know a network. A connector executes one rendered probe and returns its rows as plain dicts; everything else (rendering, fusion, judging, timeouts' meaning) is FactLang's. Every code block on this page runs in the test suite.

docs.title: The ones that ship
docs.text:
connector for fl.DBAPIConnector(conn, dialect, paramstyle=None) any PEP 249 connection: psycopg, duckdb, snowflake-connector, redshift_connector, databricks-sql, pymysql, oracledb, pyodbc, the trino driver, clickhouse-connect's DB-API fl.SQLAlchemyConnector(engine) a SQLAlchemy engine; the dialect is inferred from engine.dialect.name fl.connect(url) builds a SQLAlchemyConnector from a URL (needs factlang[sqlalchemy]) fl.BigQueryConnector(client, project, dataset=None, maximum_bytes_billed=None) BigQuery with query parameters and a dry-run cost check fl.CallableConnector(fn, dialect, paramstyle="qmark") your own fn(sql, params) -> list[dict], for hosts that already run SQL

DBAPIConnector reads the driver's paramstyle, opens a fresh cursor per probe, cancels a statement that exceeds timeout_s where the driver allows it, and serialises statements on one connection unless the driver declares PEP 249 threadsafety >= 2. The lock is kept per connection object in a weak map; a connection that cannot be weakly referenced falls back to a map keyed by id(), which holds a strong reference to it, so such a connection stays alive for the life of the process once a DBAPIConnector has wrapped it. This is the case for sqlite3 and pyodbc connections, which are not weak-referenceable. To avoid growth, open one connection and reuse one connector for it (rather than a connection and a connector per check), so the process pins one connection, not one per call.

docs.title: Writing a connector
docs.text:
The protocol is two attributes and one method:

import duckdb
import factlang as fl
from factlang.connectors import ExecutionError, QueryResult

class LoggingConnector:
    dialect = "duckdb"
    paramstyle = "qmark"

    def __init__(self, conn):
        self.conn = conn
        self.log = []

    def execute(self, probe, *, timeout_s):
        sql, params = probe.bind(self.paramstyle)   # never splice values yourself
        self.log.append(sql)
        try:
            cursor = self.conn.execute(sql, params)
        except duckdb.Error as exc:
            raise ExecutionError(str(exc), code="FL700") from exc
        names = [d[0] for d in cursor.description]
        return QueryResult(rows=[dict(zip(names, row)) for row in cursor.fetchall()])

conn = duckdb.connect()
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE orders AS SELECT range AS id FROM range(10)")
connector = LoggingConnector(conn)
outcome = fl.check("ROWS orders VALUE ==10", connector=connector, catalog=fl.NullCatalog())
assert outcome.verdict is fl.Verdict.PASS and len(connector.log) == 1

Rules:

  • Bind with probe.bind(self.paramstyle); return every row as a dict keyed by column label.
  • Raise ExecutionError with FL700 (failed), FL701 (over a cost budget) or FL702 (timeout). Anything else you raise is mapped to FL700; it becomes an error outcome, and never a no_data one.
  • Optional: dry_run_bytes(probe) -> int | None prices a probe without running it; it powers max_bytes and Checker.estimate.
  • Optional: async def aexecute(probe, *, timeout_s) makes an AsyncConnector for Checker.acheck.

docs.title: Hosts that run SQL themselves
docs.text:
connector = fl.CallableConnector(
    lambda sql, params: [dict(zip(("row_count",), conn.execute(sql, params).fetchone()))],
    "duckdb",
)
assert fl.check("ROWS orders VALUE ==10", connector=connector,
                catalog=fl.NullCatalog()).verdict is fl.Verdict.PASS

A host function cannot be handed the timeout, so enforcing it is the host's job; a TimeoutError it raises becomes FL702.

docs.text: FactLang only ever renders SELECT statements, and metadata SQL passes a keyword guard, but the connection's credentials are what really limit what can happen. Connect as a role that can only read.

docs.title: Dialects
docs.text:
Only the dialect layer knows SQL. Every IR primitive is first lowered to one internal, dialect-free SQL tree; two printers then turn that tree into text:

  1. Native profiles, the verified path. A DialectProfile is a frozen dataclass of small decisions: how to quote, how unquoted names fold, the reserved words, how to count conditionally (COUNTIF, COUNT_IF, SUM(CASE …) or FILTER), how to limit, the cast type for each type family, the clock expression, the catalog query, how to sample, and so on. Eleven ship: bigquery, snowflake, redshift, postgres, duckdb, databricks, clickhouse, tsql, mysql (also MariaDB), oracle, trino.
  2. The sqlglot bridge (pip install "factlang[sqlglot]") converts the same tree to a sqlglot expression and asks sqlglot for any other dialect: presto, athena, hive, teradata, starrocks, doris, exasol, dremio, … Its tier is best_effort.

Because both start from the same tree, they cannot disagree on what a claim means. For dialect="x" FactLang uses the native profile if one exists, else the bridge if sqlglot is installed, else FL504. Checker(..., prefer="sqlglot") forces the bridge, which is how the test suite cross-checks native SQL.

Every code block on this page runs in the test suite.

import dataclasses
import factlang as fl

print(fl.sql.native_dialects())
(probe,) = fl.compile("NULLS customers.email RATE <=5%", dialect="tsql")
print(probe.inline())
# SELECT COUNT_BIG(*) AS row_count, COUNT_BIG(email) AS non_null FROM customers

docs.title: A custom profile
docs.text:
Most engines speak a close cousin of a dialect that already has a profile. Start from that profile and change what differs:

postgres = fl.sql.get_profile("postgres")
cockroach = dataclasses.replace(
    postgres,
    name="cockroach",
    tier="native",
    sample_styles={},      # declare no table-sample method: FL506 instead of a guess
    keyhash_expr=None,     # no keyhash sampling either
)
fl.sql.register_profile(cockroach)

(probe,) = fl.compile("ROWS orders VALUE >=1", dialect="cockroach")
assert probe.dialect == "cockroach" and probe.tier == "native"

register_profile raises on an existing name unless replace=True. Template fields (information_schema_sql, sample_styles, keyhash_expr, …) are validated when the profile is built. The rare node a dialect must spell differently goes in overrides, a mapping from an internal-AST node type to a print function.

A new profile needs the conformance suite: every primitive and every metric rendered, the metric aliases unchanged (they are a wire format), and the type family table tested against that engine's type names. The repository's add-dialect skill walks through it.

docs.title: Dialect notes worth knowing
docs.text:
• Identifiers mean what they would mean in that warehouse's SQL; see Namespaces.
  • Table parts: MySQL, ClickHouse and Oracle accept two parts, the rest three (FL505).
  • SQL Server (tsql): COUNT_BIG everywhere, TOP for limits, native SUM (an overflow is an error, never a wrong number), AVG(x + 0.0) (one fractional digit lost on DECIMAL(38, s>0)). See Standard verbs.
  • Sampling support differs by dialect; see the table.
  • Casts: a JOIN … CAST <family> to a family a dialect cannot express is FL503.

docs.title: Filter and join fragments
docs.text:
Libraries built on FactLang sometimes need a piece of SQL rather than a verdict: a profiler's WHERE, a join path for a generated query. Writing it by hand would mean a second set of quoting, parameter and dialect rules that can disagree with FactLang's. Instead, parse a condition with FactLang's filter language and render it through the same internal SQL tree and identifier rules as every probe. Every code block on this page runs against DuckDB in the test suite.

import duckdb
import factlang as fl
from factlang import ColumnRef, EdgeRef, Ident, TableRef

orders = TableRef(None, None, Ident("orders"))
items = TableRef(None, None, Ident("order_items"))
customers = TableRef(None, None, Ident("customers"))

docs.title: fl.parse_filter
docs.text:
f, diagnostics = fl.parse_filter("deleted IS NULL OR NOT deleted")
assert f is not None and len(diagnostics) == 0

bad, diagnostics = fl.parse_filter("status = NULL")
print(diagnostics.render())       # error[FL206]: NULL is not a comparable value … help: use `IS NULL`
assert bad is None and diagnostics.codes() == ["FL206"]

fl.parse_filter(text, *, catalog=None, table=None) parses and analyses a bare condition (with or without a leading WHERE) and returns (FilterExpr | None, DiagnosticBag); the filter is None when there is any error. With a catalog and a table, columns are checked as in a claim (FL311, FL305 for a bare atom on a non-boolean column). Literals become parameters p1, p2, … in source order.

docs.title: fl.sql.render_filter
docs.text:
frag = fl.sql.render_filter(f, table=items, dialect="snowflake", alias="i")
print(frag.sql_template)   # (i.deleted IS NULL OR NOT (i.deleted = {{p1}}))
print(frag.inline())       # (i.deleted IS NULL OR NOT (i.deleted = TRUE))
sql, params = frag.bind("qmark")

The result is a RenderedFragment: sql_template with neutral {{name}} placeholders, params, dialect, tier, plus bind(paramstyle) and inline() exactly like a probe. It is a boolean expression, not a statement, and FactLang never executes it. alias qualifies the columns; param_prefix renames the parameters so several fragments can share a statement.

docs.title: fl.sql.render_join
docs.text:
path = [
    EdgeRef(ColumnRef(items, Ident("order_id")), ColumnRef(orders, Ident("id"))),
    EdgeRef(ColumnRef(orders, Ident("customer_id")), ColumnRef(customers, Ident("id"))),
]
snippet = fl.sql.render_join(path, dialect="duckdb", filters={items: f})
print(snippet.inline())
# FROM order_items t1 INNER JOIN orders t2 ON t1.order_id = t2.id
#   INNER JOIN customers t3 ON t2.customer_id = t3.id
#   WHERE (t1.deleted IS NULL OR NOT (t1.deleted = TRUE))

render_join(edges, dialect, *, filters=None, aliases=None) produces FROM a JOIN b ON … [JOIN c ON …] [WHERE …] for a path of EdgeRefs or fl.sql.JoinEdges (composite keys and cast_to allowed). The rule for filters: the left-most table's filter becomes the WHERE; every other table's filter is ANDed into the ON of the join that brings it in.

It is bindable, so a host can wrap it:

conn = duckdb.connect()
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE customers AS SELECT range AS id FROM range(1, 4)")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE orders AS SELECT range AS id, range AS customer_id FROM range(1, 4)")
conn.execute("""CREATE TABLE order_items AS
    SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, NULL), (2, FALSE), (3, TRUE)) AS t(order_id, deleted)""")

sql, params = snippet.bind("qmark")
count = conn.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) {sql}", params).fetchone()[0]
assert count == 2      # the deleted item is filtered out

Every native profile renders both functions; another dialect name goes through the sqlglot bridge. A hostile literal stays a parameter in every dialect.

docs.title: Packs
docs.text:
A pack is a named, versioned set of contracts. The standard pack is standard version 1.0; your own verbs live in a pack that extends it. Every code block on this page runs in the test suite.

import factlang as fl

pack = fl.standard_pack().extend("mine", "1.0")   # copy-on-write child: standard is untouched
pack.alias("CNT", "COUNT")                       # a second name for a verb
pack.remove("DEAD")                              # hide a verb in this pack only

assert fl.lint("CNT orders VALUE >=1", pack=pack).codes() == []
assert fl.lint("DEAD orders.legacy_flag", pack=pack).codes() == ["FL300"]
assert fl.lint("DEAD orders.legacy_flag").codes() == []   # the standard pack still has it

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
operation does register(contract) adds a Contract; raises if the name is taken override(contract) replaces a verb and keeps the replaced one in pack.overridden[name] alias(new, target) adds a second name; the alias analyses and hashes as its target remove(name) removes or hides a verb extend(name, version) a child pack that sees the parent's verbs and can change them without touching the parent merge(other, on_conflict="error" \| "keep" \| "replace") adds another pack's verbs; error is atomic verb(name, …) the decorator API of New verbs get(name), names(), contracts() inspection

Overriding is how you change a standard verb's behaviour, for example to tighten what UNIQUE reports, while keeping every other verb:

from dataclasses import replace

strict = fl.standard_pack().extend("strict", "1.0")
unique = strict.get("UNIQUE")
strict.override(replace(unique, spec=replace(unique.spec, summary="No key repeats, ever.")))
assert strict.overridden["UNIQUE"] is unique

docs.title: Distributing a pack
docs.text:
Expose a zero-argument factory under the factlang.packs entry-point group in your package's pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."factlang.packs"]
mine = "my_project.factlang_pack:build_pack"

fl.discover_packs() returns {name: factory} for every installed pack; calling a factory loads it:

for name, factory in fl.discover_packs().items():
    assert isinstance(factory(), fl.ContractPack), name

docs.title: Testing a pack
docs.text:
from factlang import check_pack

assert check_pack(strict) == []

check_pack runs every example of every contract and checks the completeness rules (FL600–FL605, FL404); see New verbs.

docs.title: IR primitives
docs.text: Between a claim and its SQL sits a small, dialect-free intermediate representation: a handful of measurement primitives. A verb's plan returns one; the dialect layer renders it; the engine shapes the rows by the primitive's declared arity (one row, or a row set) instead of assuming rows[0]. Every code block on this page runs in the test suite.

docs.title: The core set
docs.text:
primitive fields arity result columns ColumnAggregate table, column (or None for table metrics), metrics, filter, sample single row the metric aliases CompositeKeyAggregate table, columns, metrics, filter, sample single row the metric aliases ValueMembership table, column, declared (text; may be empty), split, report_limit (default 20, max 1000), filter, sample row set one kind='summary' row (non_null, declared_rows, undeclared_distinct) plus up to report_limit kind='undeclared' rows (value, freq), by count desc, value asc KeyOverlap left, right (equal-length tuples of column refs, one table per side), cast_to, measure_multiplicity, filter (left), right_filter, sample, right_sample single row distinct_left, matched, distinct_right, left_non_null, matched_left_rows (+ max_left_per_key, max_right_per_key) PatternCoverage table, column, pattern, filter, sample single row non_null, matching MetadataQuery table, column row set column_name, data_type

All are frozen dataclasses in factlang.ir, as are Metric, SampleSpec and Arity.

docs.title: Wire format
docs.text:
Metric result columns are a wire format, pinned by a conformance test on every dialect:

metric alias ROW_COUNT row_count NON_NULL non_null DISTINCT_KEYS distinct_keys MAX_PER_KEY max_rows_per_key MIN_VALUE min_value MAX_VALUE max_value SUM sum_value AVG avg_value DUPLICATE_KEYS duplicate_keys NOW server_now

(Never rows: it is reserved in BigQuery.)

docs.title: NULL rules live in the IR
docs.text:
So every dialect inherits them: MAX_PER_KEY excludes rows with any NULL key column before grouping; DISTINCT_KEYS over several columns groups by them and never concatenates; NON_NULL over a tuple counts rows with a complete key; PatternCoverage matches case-folded over non-NULL values; ValueMembership excludes NULLs and, with split, compares the trimmed prefix before the first separator.

No primitive limits or samples its input unless its sample field is set, which only raw measurement accepts. The one permitted limit is ValueMembership.report_limit, which truncates the ranked list of undeclared values after exact aggregation.

import factlang as fl
from factlang import Ident, TableRef

orders = TableRef(None, None, Ident("orders"))
plan = fl.ir.ColumnAggregate(orders, Ident("amount"), (fl.Metric.SUM, fl.Metric.NON_NULL))
print(plan.result_columns())          # ('sum_value', 'non_null')
probe = fl.sql.renderer_for("snowflake")(plan)
print(probe.inline())                 # SELECT SUM(amount) AS sum_value, COUNT(amount) AS non_null FROM orders
assert plan.result_columns() == ("sum_value", "non_null")

docs.title: A custom primitive
docs.text:
A plugin primitive is a frozen dataclass with a class attribute arity and a result_columns() method, registered together with a lowering into the internal SQL AST (factlang.sql.ast). Because it is lowered into the same tree as the core primitives, every native profile and the sqlglot bridge can render it, and user values can only enter through ParamRef bind parameters.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import ClassVar

from factlang.sql import Param
from factlang.sql import ast as A

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CountAbove:
    """Rows whose column exceeds a threshold."""
    arity: ClassVar[fl.ir.Arity] = fl.ir.Arity.SINGLE_ROW
    table: TableRef
    column: Ident
    threshold: Decimal

    def result_columns(self):
        return ("above",)

def lower_count_above(plan):
    above = A.Compare(">", A.Column(plan.column),
                      A.ParamRef(Param("p1", plan.threshold, "decimal")))
    return A.Select((A.Aliased(A.CountIf(above), "above"),), A.TableName(plan.table))

fl.ir.register_primitive(CountAbove, lower=lower_count_above, replace=True)

probe = fl.sql.renderer_for("bigquery")(CountAbove(orders, Ident("amount"), Decimal("100")))
print(probe.inline())    # SELECT COALESCE(COUNTIF(amount > 100), 0) AS above FROM orders
assert probe.sql_template.count("{{p1}}") == 1

A lowering that returns something other than a Select/UnionAll, or selects columns other than result_columns(), is refused with FL500, as is rendering a primitive nobody registered. Use it from a verb's plan or measure it directly.

fl.ir.unregister_primitive(cls) removes a registration (in a test's teardown, say) and raises KeyError if cls has none. Change the registry only through these two functions: fl.ir.PRIMITIVE_LOWERINGS is read-only by convention. It stays a plain dict throughout 0.1.x; a read-only view is planned for 0.2.0.

fl.ir.unregister_primitive(CountAbove)
assert CountAbove not in fl.ir.PRIMITIVE_LOWERINGS
fl.ir.register_primitive(CountAbove, lower=lower_count_above)  # no replace=True needed now

docs.title: Value types
docs.text:
Every attribute has a value type that says which literal kinds it accepts and how a literal becomes a Python value. The built-in types include NUMBER, INTEGER, RATIO (percentages normalised, 0 to 1), DURATION, STRING, SYMBOL, TYPE_FAMILY, CARDINALITY, COLUMN_LIST, VALUE_LIST, RANGE_PAIR, SEPARATOR and LIKE_PATTERN. Every code block on this page runs in the test suite.

A ValueType has four parts:

field name uppercase, used in fl.Attr(name, "<TYPE>") accepts the literal kinds allowed; anything else is FL305 coerce(literal) turns the literal into a value; returns fl.types.Invalid(message) instead of raising validate(value) returns an error message (reported as FL309) or None

docs.title: A custom type
docs.text:
import factlang as fl
LiteralKind = fl.types.LiteralKind

def domain(literal):
    text = str(literal.value).lower()
    return text if "." in text else fl.types.Invalid(f"{text!r} is not a domain name")

fl.types.register(
    fl.types.ValueType("EMAIL_DOMAIN", frozenset({LiteralKind.STRING}), coerce=domain),
    replace=True,
)

pack = fl.standard_pack().extend("mail", "1.0")

@pack.verb(
    "MAIL_DOMAIN",
    summary="Every e-mail address of the column ends with the domain.",
    operands=[fl.Operand.column()],
    attrs=[fl.Attr("IS", "EMAIL_DOMAIN", required=True)],
)
def mail_domain(claim):
    pattern = "%@" + claim.value("IS")
    return fl.ir.PatternCoverage(claim.table, claim.column.column, pattern)

@mail_domain.derive
def _(payload, claim):
    return {"match_rate": None if not payload["non_null"] else payload["matching"] / payload["non_null"]}

mail_domain.facts("match_rate").decide(fl.Compare("match_rate", "==", value=1))

assert fl.lint("MAIL_DOMAIN customers.email IS 'example.com'", pack=pack).codes() == []
assert fl.lint("MAIL_DOMAIN customers.email IS 'localhost'", pack=pack).codes() == ["FL309"]
assert fl.lint("MAIL_DOMAIN customers.email IS 42", pack=pack).codes() == ["FL305"]

The registry is process-wide. Registering an existing name raises unless replace=True.

docs.title: New verbs
docs.text:
A verb is data, not grammar: the parser accepts VERB operands ATTRIBUTES [WHERE …] for any uppercase verb, and the analyser checks the line against the verb's signature. Adding a verb means writing one contract:

part job signature operands, attributes (with value types and allowed operators), whether WHERE is accepted plan turns a checked claim into an IR primitive: what to measure derive turns the measured row(s) into named facts; returns None for a fact the data cannot support decide a predicate over the facts: the verdict examples at least three valid and three invalid claims, executed by the tests

Every code block on this page runs against DuckDB in the test suite.

docs.title: A verb in a dozen lines
docs.text:
POSITIVE t.c claims that every non-NULL value of a column is above zero.

import duckdb
import factlang as fl

pack = fl.standard_pack().extend("mine", "1.0")

@pack.verb(
    "POSITIVE",
    summary="Every non-NULL value of the column is greater than zero.",
    operands=[fl.Operand.column()],
    filterable=True,
)
def positive(claim):
    return fl.ir.ColumnAggregate(
        claim.table, claim.column, [fl.Metric.MIN_VALUE], filter=claim.filter
    )

@positive.derive
def _(payload, claim):
    return {"min": payload["min_value"]}

positive.facts("min")
positive.decide(fl.Compare("min", ">", value=0))
positive.example("POSITIVE orders.amount")
positive.example("POSITIVE order_items.price WHERE status = 'paid'")
positive.example("POSITIVE shop.orders.amount")
positive.example("POSITIVE orders", valid=False, expect="FL302")
positive.example("POSITIVE orders.amount VALUE > 0", valid=False, expect="FL303")
positive.example("POSITIVE orders.amount WHERE", valid=False, expect="FL206")

Use it by passing the pack to a Checker (or to fl.lint / fl.compile):

conn = duckdb.connect()
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER, amount DECIMAL(10, 2), status VARCHAR)")
conn.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 5.00, 'paid'), (2, -1.00, 'void'), (3, NULL, 'open')")
checker = fl.Checker(fl.DBAPIConnector(conn, "duckdb"), pack=pack)

report = checker.check("POSITIVE orders.amount\nPOSITIVE orders.amount WHERE status = 'paid'")
for o in report.outcomes:
    print(o.verdict.value, o.explanation)
# fail min -1 <= 0
# pass min 5 > 0
assert [o.verdict.value for o in report.outcomes] == ["fail", "pass"]

docs.title: Rules the tests enforce
docs.text:
Run fl.check_pack(pack) in your own test suite; it returns a list of problems, empty when the pack is complete:

from factlang import check_pack

assert check_pack(pack) == []

It reports:

  • FL600: decide reads a fact that derive never declares (.facts(...)).
  • FL601: decide reads an attribute the signature does not declare.
  • FL602: fewer than three valid and three invalid examples.
  • FL603: an example does not behave as declared (or its plan raises). A plan must return a probe plan: a core primitive or an instance of a class registered with fl.ir.register_primitive. One that returns None or anything else is refused with a ValueError naming the verb, and check() reports the claim as error ("plan failed").
  • FL604: a decorator-built contract is missing a part (plan, derive or decide).
  • FL605: a filterable verb's plan drops the claim's WHERE filter. A plan that ignores claim.filter would measure the whole table while the claim talks about some of it, so always pass filter=claim.filter on.
  • FL404: the plan sets sample. Claims are always measured exactly.

docs.title: Attributes and predicates
docs.text:
Attributes are declared with fl.Attr(name, type, required=False, ops=(), doc=""), where type names a value type (NUMBER, INTEGER, RATIO, DURATION, STRING, SYMBOL, COLUMN_LIST, …) and ops lists the operators the attribute accepts (empty: it takes none). The predicate language is small on purpose, so a verdict always explains itself:

predicate decides Compare(fact, op, value=…) a fact against a constant Compare(fact, op, attr="NAME") a fact against an attribute of the claim, with a fixed operator CompareUsingClaimOp(fact, "NAME") a fact against the attribute, using the operator the author wrote Within(fact, "VALUE") like the above, with the claim's TOLERANCE / ABS_TOLERANCE band And(...), Or(...), Not(p) three-valued combinations: None stays undecidable WhenClaimHas("NAME", p) applies p only when the claim carries the attribute 
@pack.verb(
    "LOWEST",
    summary="The smallest non-NULL value of the column satisfies the stated comparison.",
    operands=[fl.Operand.column()],
    attrs=[fl.Attr("VALUE", "NUMBER", required=True, ops=("==", "<=", "<", ">=", ">"))],
    filterable=True,
)
def lowest(claim):
    return fl.ir.ColumnAggregate(
        claim.table, claim.column, [fl.Metric.MIN_VALUE], filter=claim.filter
    )

@lowest.derive
def _(payload, claim):
    return {"lowest": payload["min_value"]}  # None over no rows: the verdict is no_data

lowest.facts("lowest")
lowest.decide(fl.CompareUsingClaimOp("lowest", "VALUE"))
lowest.example("LOWEST orders.amount VALUE >= 0")
lowest.example("LOWEST orders.amount VALUE == 5 WHERE status = 'paid'")
lowest.example("LOWEST shop.orders.amount VALUE < 100")
lowest.example("LOWEST orders.amount", valid=False, expect="FL304")
lowest.example("LOWEST orders.amount VALUE 0", valid=False, expect="FL306")
lowest.example("LOWEST orders.amount VALUE >= 'x'", valid=False, expect="FL305")

report = checker.check("LOWEST orders.amount VALUE >= -1\nLOWEST orders.amount VALUE >= 0")
assert [o.verdict.value for o in report.outcomes] == ["pass", "fail"]
assert check_pack(pack) == []

Writing a contract as a Contract(...) object instead of with the decorator gives the same result; the standard verbs are written that way, one file per verb, and make good templates.

docs.title: Catalog and semantic verbs
docs.text: A verb answered from the catalog uses .catalog(fn) instead of a plan (fn(claim, catalog) returns the facts); a verb no query can establish uses .unprobeable("reason") and is reported as unprobeable, like NOTE. Exactly one of plan, catalog and unprobeable is set.

docs.title: Batching and fusion
docs.text:
FactLang is built for warehouses where a scan costs money and a catalog has hundreds of thousands of schemas. A Checker checks a whole document at once and does as little work as it can without ever giving up exactness.

import factlang as fl

checker = fl.Checker(
    connector,          # any Connector; or dialect="…" alone to compile without one
    catalog=None,       # default: CachedCatalog(WarehouseCatalog(connector))
    concurrency=4,      # probes in flight at once
    timeout_s=60,       # per probe; a timeout is an `error` outcome with FL702
    max_bytes=None,     # cost budget, enforced through the connector's dry run
    fuse=True,          # share scans between claims (see below)
)
report = checker.check(open("facts.fl").read())

docs.title: De-duplication
docs.text: Claims with the same semantic hash are measured once, even when spelled differently or written under different USE lines. Each still gets its own outcome.

docs.title: Fusion
docs.text:
Aggregate claims over the same table with the same filter are fused into one SELECT that computes all their metrics, with aliases prefixed m<i>__, and the result row is split back per claim. These three claims are one scan:

ROWS orders VALUE >=1
NULLS orders.shipped_at RATE <=50%
MAX orders.amount VALUE <=204

SELECT COUNT(*) AS m0__row_count, COUNT(*) AS m1__row_count,
       COUNT(shipped_at) AS m1__non_null, MAX(amount) AS m2__max_value
FROM orders

Each outcome's evidence.fused_with lists the semantic hashes of its scan partners, and its evidence.sql is the fused statement that actually ran. Claims with different filters are never fused, so no claim's numbers can be affected by another claim's rows. fuse=False gives every claim its own query.

docs.title: Concurrency, timeouts and cost
docs.text:
Probes run concurrency at a time, on a thread pool for check and an asyncio semaphore for acheck (await checker.acheck(text), with an AsyncConnector). A connector that cannot enforce timeout_s itself is backstopped: no answer a few seconds after the timeout is reported as FL702 and abandoned.

With max_bytes set and a connector that supports a dry run (BigQuery does), each probe is priced first; a probe over budget is never executed and becomes an error outcome with FL701. To price a document without running anything, ask for an estimate:

for estimate in checker.estimate("JOIN orders.customer_id -> customers.id MATCH >=99%"):
    print(estimate.key, estimate.method, estimate.bytes)

A connector without a dry run returns bytes=None, method="unknown"; FactLang never guesses a price.

docs.title: Catalogs never enumerate
docs.text: Name checks and the structure verbs ask the catalog about the tables your claims mention, one table at a time, and cache the answers. Nothing ever lists every schema. See Catalogs.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
A verdict you cannot audit is just another claim. Every measured outcome carries an Evidence record:

field sql the query, display form: literals inlined, ready to paste into a console; the {{name}} template when a literal cannot be inlined safely params the values that were bound as typed parameters when the query actually ran dialect the dialect it was rendered for tier how much that rendering is trusted: verified, native or best_effort duration_ms wall-clock time of the query bytes_processed when the connector reports it (BigQuery does) fused_with semantic hashes of the other claims answered by the same query method exact for every claim; sampled:<method>:<fraction>:<seed> only for raw sampled measurements

docs.title: What runs is not what you read
docs.text:
The executed statement is a template with neutral placeholders plus an ordered tuple of typed parameters. fl.compile shows both:

import factlang as fl

(probe,) = fl.compile("COUNT orders VALUE ==1400 WHERE status = 'paid'", dialect="postgres")
print(probe.sql_template)
# SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM orders WHERE status = CAST({{p1}} AS TEXT)
print(probe.params)
# (Param(name='p1', value='paid', family='string'),)
print(probe.bind("pyformat"))
# ('SELECT … WHERE status = CAST(%(p1)s AS TEXT)', {'p1': 'paid'})
print(probe.inline())
# SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM orders WHERE status = CAST('paid' AS TEXT)

Parameters carry their type family, and some profiles (Postgres here) cast each placeholder to that type explicitly. bind(paramstyle) produces the driver's spelling for qmark, numeric, named, format or pyformat; each connector declares its own.

Two guards hold on every rendered probe: it begins with SELECT or WITH, and it contains no ; outside a literal. Identifiers that cannot be represented safely (a NUL or newline, or longer than the dialect allows) are refused with FL502, never sanitised.

docs.title: Inlining is display-oriented, and fails closed
docs.text:
inline() is for people: FactLang never executes it. Because a host might still run it (a driver that cannot bind, a console paste), it is built to be safe if executed, and refuses whatever it cannot render safely instead of guessing:

  • Strings are quoted by doubling ', in every dialect. Nothing relies on backslash escaping, so a string literal does not depend on string-escape settings (MySQL's default sql_mode, PostgreSQL's standard_conforming_strings).
  • A string holding a backslash, a NUL, a lone surrogate or a line terminator (CR, LF, U+0085, U+2028, U+2029) is refused, as is a ' in a dialect whose lexer does not read '' as a quote. That is decided by the dialect the renderer resolves: a native profile's doubled_quote_escape (False for bigquery and databricks), or, for a bridged dialect, sqlglot's own tokenizer (so spark, spark2 and hive refuse it too). A dialect nothing knows refuses it. A custom profile defaults to False, and when its name is also a dialect sqlglot knows, doubling is used only if that dialect's lexer reads '' as a quote too (a postgres-like profile registered as hive still refuses ').
  • Only values of an exact built-in type are inlined: None, bool, int, float, Decimal, str, datetime.date and datetime.datetime. A subclass of any of them (an IntEnum, a numpy scalar, a str subclass) is refused, because its own methods could print anything; values are rendered through the base type's functions or from their fields. Lists, dicts, sets, bytes, other objects, NaN, infinities and a value whose type does not match its parameter family (a datetime in a date parameter, True in an integer one) are refused.
  • Numbers are inlined only where every engine reads the literal as that exact value: an int within the signed 64-bit range, and a Decimal whose plain form needs a precision (integer digits plus scale, what DECIMAL(p,s) must hold) of at most 38, so Decimal('1E+50') (precision 51) is refused. Past those limits engines silently change the literal's type or precision (DuckDB reads a 39-digit fraction as DOUBLE, a 20-digit integer as HUGEINT). A finite float always inlines: its shortest repr never has more than 17 significant digits. Bound parameters have no such limits.

  • Spellings follow the dialect. T-SQL strings are national literals (N'…'); T-SQL, Oracle and Teradata booleans are 1/0. Timestamps are converted to UTC; fractional seconds (.ffffff) are written only when the microseconds are not zero. Dates are DATE '…' everywhere except T-SQL (CAST('…' AS DATE)).

    Timestamp literals:

    • trino, databricks, and bridged presto, athena, spark and Trino-derived dialects: TIMESTAMP 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS[.ffffff] UTC';
    • bridged spark2: CAST('YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS[.ffffff]Z' AS TIMESTAMP);
    • oracle, and bridged hive, teradata, exasol: TIMESTAMP 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS[.ffffff]';
    • tsql (and bridged fabric): CAST('YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS[.ffffff]' AS DATETIME2);
    • every other dialect: TIMESTAMP 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.ffffff]+00:00'.

    A bridged dialect takes its spellings from a small internal table of sqlglot dialect names (BRIDGE_LITERAL_STYLES in factlang.sql.sqlglot_bridge, not public API), else from the nearest native profile it derives from in sqlglot (Fabric from T-SQL, Materialize from Postgres), else the ANSI forms. Whether '' may be used is always decided by the dialect's own lexer. - The spelling follows what the dialect's TIMESTAMP type is. Where it is zone-aware or session-time-zone-local, the literal carries an explicit UTC zone, so it is the UTC instant whatever the session time zone: Trino, Presto and Athena (TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE), and Databricks and Spark (Spark 3.0 and later), which read a zone-less literal in the session time zone (spark.sql.session.timeZone). Spark 2.x (spark2) reads a zone-less literal in the JVM default zone, and its TIMESTAMP '…' literal form (java.sql.Timestamp.valueOf) rejects a zone suffix, so it inlines a cast of a Z-suffixed string instead, which Spark's string-to-timestamp cast reads as UTC. Before 0.1.4 all three were zone-less and named another instant under a non-UTC session or JVM zone. Where it is zone-less (a local date-time: Hive, Teradata, Exasol, Oracle), a naive literal holding UTC wall-clock time is the correct value. Elsewhere a timestamp inlines as a literal most engines read as a naive (time-zone-less) value holding UTC wall-clock time; compared with a time-zone-aware column (timestamptz, DATETIMEOFFSET, TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE), the result then depends on the session time zone, as it does for the bound parameter. The executed statement always binds its parameters, so the inline spelling never changes what a check measures.

A refusal is RenderError("FL507 cannot inline <type> parameter <name> …"). Evidence never fails a check over it: evidence.sql (and factlang explain, the agent's factlang_explain and Checker.estimate) shows the template with its {{name}} placeholders instead, and the values are in params; any other exception raised while converting a value is treated the same way. The claim itself is judged exactly as before, because the executed statement always binds its parameters. (FL500 stays a genuine render bug and is never swallowed.)

What inline text assumes

Inline text is for display, and for hosts that cannot bind parameters. Bind whenever you can. The literals assume the client connection uses UTF-8 (or a single-byte character set in which every byte is a whole character): a multi-byte client charset such as SJIS, Big5 or GBK talking to a server that also honours backslash escapes is out of scope. Console tools may reinterpret pasted text before the server sees it: SQL*Plus substitutes &name and, by default (SQLBLANKLINES OFF), a blank line ends the SQL being entered even inside a string literal, so the lines after it run as a new command (which is why no inlined literal holds a line terminator); SSMS and sqlcmd split batches at a line holding GO, and drivers that parse paramstyle markers can read a %s, %(name)s or ? inside a literal as a placeholder. Pass inline text to such a tool only after checking it.

import factlang as fl

from factlang.engine import display_sql

(probe,) = fl.compile(r"COUNT orders VALUE ==0 WHERE status = 'a\b'", dialect="mysql")
try:
    probe.inline()
except fl.sql.RenderError as exc:
    print(exc)  # FL507 cannot inline str parameter p1: it contains a backslash or NUL, ...
print(display_sql(probe))
# SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM orders WHERE status = {{p1}}
assert display_sql(probe) == probe.sql_template

docs.text:
tier dialects what it means verified duckdb, postgres, mysql, clickhouse, tsql, trino the native SQL is executed against a real engine in CI, verb by verb native bigquery, snowflake, redshift, databricks, oracle native SQL checked by parsing it with sqlglot in that dialect and by golden tests; an opt-in live suite runs it when credentials are present best_effort any other name sqlglot knows (presto, athena, hive, teradata, …) rendered through the optional sqlglot bridge (pip install "factlang[sqlglot]")

The tier is reported on every outcome, so a host can, for example, accept a best_effort pass only after a human has looked at the SQL.

docs.title: No sampling in claims
docs.text:
A claim's numbers are computed over all rows matching its filter. No claim, contract or analyser ever produces a sampled plan; a contract that tries is a bug, reported as FL404. The only row limit in any claim query is the length of the ranked list of undeclared values that VALUES reports, applied after exact aggregation. The conformance suite asserts that no LIMIT, TOP, FETCH FIRST, SAMPLE or TABLESAMPLE appears anywhere else.

Why so strict: LIMIT returns rows in storage order, not at random, and a "sampled" probe once reported a 22.5% rate against an exact 6.8%.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Every measurable verb accepts a WHERE filter that restricts the rows it measures. The filter is always the last element of a claim and runs to the end of the line.

COUNT orders VALUE ==1400 WHERE status = 'paid'
NULLS orders.shipped_at RATE <=1% WHERE status IN ['paid', 'refunded']
ROWS events VALUE >=1 WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01T00:00:00Z'
UNIQUE customers.email WHERE deleted IS NULL OR NOT deleted

Because the filter always comes last, attribute names such as IN, IS, BETWEEN and NOT can double as filter keywords with no ambiguity. Write attributes first: COUNT orders VALUE ==1400 WHERE status = 'paid', never COUNT orders WHERE status = 'paid' VALUE ==1400 (that is FL206: the filter would have to swallow VALUE).

docs.title: The condition language
docs.text:
condition  = conj { OR conj }
conj       = atom { AND atom }
atom       = NOT atom | ( condition ) | comparison | name
comparison = name OP literal
           | name IN [ ... ]          | name NOT IN [ ... ]
           | name IS NULL             | name IS NOT NULL
           | name BETWEEN literal AND literal
literal    = number | 'string' | TRUE | FALSE | DATE '…' | TIMESTAMP '…'
  • Precedence from loosest to tightest: OR, AND, NOT. Use parentheses when in doubt.
  • OP is one of = == != < <= > >=.
  • The left side of a comparison is a single column of the claim's (left) table, never a dotted ref and never an expression.
  • x IS NULL is the only test for NULL. x = NULL is FL206, because in SQL it is never true.
  • Filter keywords are recognised in uppercase only. A column whose name is a keyword must be quoted: WHERE "status" = 'x' is fine, and so is WHERE "NULL" = 1.

docs.title: Bare boolean columns
docs.text:
A column name standing alone tests a boolean column for truth: WHERE deleted means WHERE deleted = TRUE, and NOT deleted means NOT (deleted = TRUE). Under SQL's three-valued logic NOT deleted excludes rows where deleted is NULL, so the idiomatic live-row filter for a flag that is TRUE or NULL is:

ROWS orders VALUE >=1 WHERE deleted IS NULL OR NOT deleted

When a catalog knows the column is not boolean, the analyser reports FL305. A bare TRUE or FALSE atom is FL206; they are keywords, not names.

docs.title: Literals are typed bind parameters
docs.text:
Every literal in a filter becomes a typed bind parameter, named p1, p2, … in source order: a number becomes an integer or decimal parameter, a string a string, TRUE/FALSE a boolean, DATE '…' a date and TIMESTAMP '…' a timestamp (no offset means UTC). An invalid ISO date such as DATE '2026-02-30' is FL309. No literal is ever spliced into SQL text, so this filter is harmless:

ROWS orders VALUE ==0 WHERE status = 'x''; DROP TABLE orders; --'

docs.title: Which verbs accept a filter
docs.text:
Filterable: ROWS NULLS UNIQUE FANOUT VALUES RANGE PATTERN FRESH JOIN COUNT DISTINCT SUM AVG MIN MAX. Not filterable: EXISTS TYPE DEAD NOTE (FL308). On a JOIN, the filter applies to the left table.

A filter is part of a claim's identity: ROWS orders VALUE >=1 and the same claim with WHERE status = 'paid' are different facts with different semantic hashes. Claims over the same table with the same filter share one scan (see Batching).

docs.title: Filters without a claim
docs.text: Libraries that need FactLang's filter language for their own SQL can parse a bare condition and render it for any dialect; see Filter and join fragments.

docs.title: The language
docs.text: A FactLang document is a list of lines. Each line is a claim (one fact about the warehouse), a USE directive (a default namespace), a comment or blank. This page explains the shape of a claim; the grammar reference is the normative definition, and every example in it is executed by the test suite.

docs.title: Anatomy of a claim
docs.text:
JOIN orders.customer_id -> customers.id CARD N:1 MATCH >=99% WHERE status = 'paid'
part here rule verb JOIN the first token; an all-uppercase word, checked against the active pack operands orders.customer_id -> customers.id refs, edges (a -> b) or literals; they end at the first uppercase word attributes CARD N:1, MATCH >=99% an uppercase name, an optional operator, a value filter WHERE status = 'paid' optional, always last, runs to the end of the line

The grammar knows no verbs. It parses VERB operands ATTRIBUTES [WHERE …] for any verb, and the analyser then checks the line against the verb's signature. That is why adding a verb is data, never a change to the parser (see New verbs).

docs.title: One claim per line
docs.text:
A claim ends at the newline. A file with five mistakes reports five diagnostics: after an error the parser skips to the next line and carries on. A trailing backslash continues a claim, which long value lists need:

VALUES orders.status IN ['new', 'paid', 'packed', 'shipped', \
                         'delivered', 'returned', 'refunded']

# starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. Comments are kept by the formatter and ignored by everything else.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
A reference names a table or a column with one to four dot-separated parts:

written means orders a table, in the connection's default schema shop.orders schema shop, table orders analytics.shop.orders catalog (database, project) analytics, schema shop orders.id column id of table orders analytics.shop.orders.id the same column, fully qualified

Whether a ref is a table or a column is decided by the verb's signature: ROWS takes a table, UNIQUE a column. In a column ref the last part is always the column, and the table parts fill the slots catalog, schema, table from the right. What the slots mean on your warehouse (a BigQuery project, a Snowflake database, a MySQL database) and how many it accepts is a property of the dialect; see Namespaces.

docs.title: Identifiers mean what they mean in your SQL
docs.text:
An unquoted identifier is written to the SQL unquoted, so the warehouse applies its own case rules: orders finds ORDERS on Snowflake exactly as your own SQL would. A quoted identifier keeps its case and may contain spaces:

ROWS "Order Items" VALUE >=1
UNIQUE `legacy-orders`.id

Double quotes and backticks both delimit identifiers; FactLang writes them with your dialect's quote character. Strings use single quotes only, with '' for a quote inside a string, as in SQL.

Uppercase operands

Operands end at the first all-uppercase bare word, so an uppercase table name must be quoted: ROWS "ORDERS" VALUE >=1. Without the quotes, ORDERS would be read as an attribute.

docs.title: Writing names from code
docs.text:
A program that generates claims from warehouse metadata does not have to re-derive these rules: factlang.syntax.needs_quoting(name) says whether a name written bare would denote something else (an uppercase word, a filter keyword, a space or a leading digit), and factlang.syntax.quote_name(name) returns its double-quoted form, refusing (ValueError) an empty name or one holding a carriage return, a newline or NUL.

import factlang as fl
from factlang.syntax import needs_quoting, quote_name

def name(n: str) -> str:
    return quote_name(n) if needs_quoting(n) else n

print(name("status"), name("ID"), name("order items"), name('say "hi"'))
# status "ID" "order items" "say ""hi"""
assert fl.lint(f"UNIQUE {name('Order Items')}.{name('ID')}").has_errors is False

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
kind examples notes number 1717, 1_717, -3.5, 1e6 _ groups digits percent 99%, 0.5% normalised to a ratio at parse time: 99% is 0.99 duration 30s, 15m, 24h, 7d, 2w normalised to seconds string 'paid', 'O''Brien' single quotes cardinality 1:1, 1:N, N:1, N:M one token typed DATE '2025-01-31', TIMESTAMP '2025-01-31T12:00:00Z' ISO 8601; no offset means UTC list ['a', 'b'], [line_no, shop_id] a trailing comma is allowed symbol integer, string, bytes a bare lowercase word, e.g. a type family

An attribute's operator is one of == != < <= > >=; = is accepted as a synonym of ==. Each verb declares which operators an attribute accepts: RATE takes <= but not !=, and IS takes none.

docs.title: Canonical form and identity
docs.text:
fl.format prints a document in canonical form: single spaces, == for =, normalised numbers, comments kept.

import factlang as fl
print(fl.format("ROWS orders VALUE=1_717   # yesterday's count"))
# ROWS orders VALUE == 1717  # yesterday's count

Every claim also has a semantic hash: SHA-256 over the verb, the resolved operands, the filter (commutative parts in canonical order) and the attributes sorted by name. It ignores comments, whitespace, attribute order, numeric spelling and = versus ==, and it is computed after USE expansion, so the same fact written two ways hashes the same. Hosts use it to deduplicate claims and to keep a history of verdicts per fact.

docs.title: Raw measurement and sampling
docs.text:
Claims answer "is this true?". Libraries built on FactLang, such as schema profilers, often need the plain numbers instead: the top values of a column, how two keys overlap, what a scan would cost. This page covers the three tools for that: raw measurement, cost estimates and metadata SQL, and the one place sampling is allowed.

Every code block on this page runs against DuckDB in the test suite.

import duckdb
import factlang as fl
from decimal import Decimal
from factlang import ColumnRef, Ident, TableRef

conn = duckdb.connect()
conn.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE orders AS
    SELECT i AS id, 1 + i % 400 AS customer_id,
           CASE i % 10 WHEN 0 THEN 'refunded' WHEN 1 THEN 'open' ELSE 'paid' END AS status
    FROM range(1, 100001) AS t(i)
""")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE customers AS SELECT i AS id FROM range(1, 501) AS t(i)")
connector = fl.DBAPIConnector(conn, "duckdb")

orders = TableRef(None, None, Ident("orders"))
customers = TableRef(None, None, Ident("customers"))

docs.title: Raw measurement
docs.text:
fl.measure (and Checker.measure / ameasure for batches) runs IR primitives that have no claim, through the same render, cost guard and execute path as claims, with fusion and de-duplication across the batch.

top = fl.measure(
    fl.ir.ValueMembership(orders, Ident("status"), declared=(), report_limit=20),
    connector=connector,
)
summary, *ranked = top.payload["rows"]
print(summary["non_null"], [(r["value"], r["freq"]) for r in ranked])
# 100000 [('paid', 80000), ('open', 10000), ('refunded', 10000)]
assert top.error is None
assert [(r["value"], r["freq"]) for r in ranked][0] == ("paid", 80000)

The first row is the summary (kind='summary': non_null, declared_rows, undeclared_distinct); the rest are kind='undeclared' rows with value and freq. With declared=() every value is undeclared, so the ranked rows are the exact top-k observed values (NULLs excluded, ranked by count, then value; report_limit up to 1000).

A Measurement has:

field plan the plan you passed payload exactly what a contract's derive would receive: the result row as a dict of wire-format aliases for single-row primitives, {"rows": [...]} for row sets, None when the query returned no rows evidence the same Evidence an outcome carries error None, or the Diagnostic (FL7xx for execution, FL4xx/FL5xx when the plan could not be rendered) verdict_hint error on an error, no_data when no rows came back, else None

Measuring never raises for an execution failure; check error.

overlap = fl.measure(
    fl.ir.KeyOverlap(
        left=(ColumnRef(orders, Ident("customer_id")),),
        right=(ColumnRef(customers, Ident("id")),),
    ),
    connector=connector,
)
print(overlap.payload)
assert overlap.payload["distinct_left"] == 400 and overlap.payload["distinct_right"] == 500

docs.title: Cost estimates
docs.text:
Checker.estimate renders claims (text) or plans and asks the connector's optional dry run for the bytes, without executing anything:

checker = fl.Checker(connector)
(estimate,) = checker.estimate("JOIN orders.customer_id -> customers.id MATCH >=99%")
print(estimate.method, estimate.bytes)    # unknown None: DuckDB has no dry run
assert estimate.bytes is None and estimate.method == "unknown"

On BigQuery (BigQueryConnector) the method is dry_run and bytes is the warehouse's own figure. A connector without a dry run never gets a guessed number.

docs.title: Metadata SQL
docs.text:
Some hosts must list schemas and tables themselves. fl.run_metadata(connector, sql, params) runs host-written catalog metadata SQL (INFORMATION_SCHEMA, system views, SHOW, DESCRIBE) through any connector, with the same execution, timeout, parameter binding and error mapping as probes. It returns a QueryResult, never an outcome.

result = fl.run_metadata(
    connector,
    "SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name = {{name}}",
    {"name": "orders"},
)
print(result.rows)                     # [{'table_name': 'orders'}]
assert result.rows == [{"table_name": "orders"}]

Values go in {{name}} parameter tokens and are bound, never spliced. Before anything runs, a guard refuses the statement with FL703 unless:

  • it is one statement whose first word is SELECT, WITH, SHOW, DESCRIBE, DESC or EXPLAIN (not EXPLAIN ANALYZE);
  • it contains none of ; ->> -- /* */ // # $ \, no Oracle q' quoting and no non-ASCII character outside parameter tokens (some engines fold Unicode case into keywords);
  • no write, DDL or control keyword (INSERT, INTO, COPY, CALL, EXEC, MERGE, GRANT, SET, USE, ATTACH, PRAGMA, …) appears anywhere as a whole word. The read-only row-limiting phrases FETCH FIRST|NEXT <n> ROW|ROWS ONLY and OFFSET <n> ROW|ROWS (<n> a number or one {{name}} token) are allowed, so Oracle 12c+ and Db2 metadata queries can limit rows; any other FETCH is refused.

What the guard is, and is not

The guard is lexer-free and deliberately over-strict. It scans the raw text without understanding quotes, so a forbidden word inside a string literal is refused too; pass such values as parameters. Modelling each dialect's lexer was rejected after review found bypasses through dollar quotes, MySQL --, Snowflake // and Oracle q'.

It is a keyword guard, not a sandbox. A side-effecting function called from a SELECT (nextval, NEXT VALUE FOR, pg_sleep, dblink_exec, pg_terminate_backend, …) is not detected. The connection's credentials are the real security boundary: run metadata SQL as a role that can only read.

The guard trusts the connector's dialect label. On tsql, where statements need no separator, only SELECT is accepted, it runs wrapped as SELECT * FROM (<sql>) AS fl_meta_q, quote characters (' " [ ]) are refused and parentheses must balance, so the wrapper cannot be escaped. A SQL Server connection labelled with another dialect name loses that protection.

docs.title: Sampling very large tables
docs.text:
Exact measurement of a terabyte table can be too slow or too expensive for a profiler. For raw measurement only, a primitive may carry a SampleSpec:

spec = fl.ir.SampleSpec("keyhash", Decimal("0.1"), seed=7, key=(Ident("customer_id"),))
sampled = fl.measure(
    fl.ir.ColumnAggregate(orders, None, (fl.Metric.ROW_COUNT,), sample=spec),
    connector=connector,
)
print(sampled.payload, sampled.evidence.method)
# {'row_count': …, 'sampled_rows': …} sampled:keyhash:0.1:7
assert sampled.evidence.method == "sampled:keyhash:0.1:7"
assert sampled.payload["row_count"] == sampled.payload["sampled_rows"] < 100000

Measurement only, never verdicts

No claim, contract or analyser ever produces a sampled plan, and no verdict (pass, fail, no_data) is ever computed from sampled data. A contract whose plan sets sample is a bug and gets FL404. LIMIT is never a sampling method.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
keyhash Keeps a row when a deterministic hash of its key columns, salted with the seed, falls in the first fraction of a million buckets. The same key always lands in the same bucket, so a kept key keeps all its rows, the same seed gives the same sample on every run, and two tables sampled on their join key with the same fraction and seed keep exactly the same key values, which is what makes sampled join measurements meaningful. Allowed on every primitive. system The warehouse's block sample (TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM, with a repeatable seed where the dialect has one). Cheap, because unread blocks are never scanned, but coarse. bernoulli The warehouse's row sample: each row is kept independently with probability fraction.

A fraction of 1 renders no sample at all. The payload holds the raw metrics of the sampled rows plus sampled_rows (sampled_left_rows and sampled_right_rows for a KeyOverlap, whose two sides take sample and right_sample). FactLang does not scale anything up: the estimate is the host's to make. Evidence records the sample and method = "sampled:<method>:<fraction>:<seed>"; exact measurements say exact.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• system and bernoulli need a single read (FL405). A ValueMembership, a KeyOverlap, or an aggregate with a keyed metric (MAX_PER_KEY, DUPLICATE_KEYS, a composite DISTINCT_KEYS) reads the sampled table more than once, and a block or row sample is not guaranteed to repeat between reads (BigQuery, for one, re-evaluates CTEs). Use keyhash for those.
  • A method the dialect cannot express is FL506, never a silent exact query or a silent LIMIT.
  • keyhash is consistent within one dialect only. Each dialect hashes with its own function, so the same seed keeps the same keys on every table of one warehouse, which is all a join needs, but not across warehouses.
  • With cast_to, sample on exactly the join columns. A KeyOverlap hashes the key as compared (after cast_to) only when a side's keyhash key equals that side's join columns, in order; any other key is hashed raw, and the two sides' raw values (of different types) then keep different keys.

docs.title: Support by dialect
docs.text:
dialect keyhash system bernoulli postgres yes (hashtextextended, PG 11+) yes yes duckdb yes FL506 yes snowflake yes FL506 yes databricks yes FL506 yes oracle yes FL506 yes tsql yes FL506 FL506 bigquery yes FL506 FL506 redshift yes FL506 FL506 mysql yes FL506 FL506 clickhouse yes FL506 FL506 trino yes FL506 FL506 sqlglot bridge FL506 unless the target is one of the above where sqlglot has TABLESAMPLE where sqlglot has TABLESAMPLE

Block sampling is refused where repeatability with a seed is not established; DuckDB's SYSTEM sample, for example, samples whole vectors and is not repeatable across threads even with a seed.
